result:
There is a particular kind of quiet that arrives just before rain.

Leaves turn their pale undersides toward the sky. Birds retreat to hidden places. The air seems to hold its breath—not from fear, but anticipation. Then the first drop darkens the pavement, another taps the window, and suddenly the whole world is speaking at once.

Rain makes ordinary things noticeable. Gutters become rivers. Streetlights shimmer in puddles. A forgotten umbrella becomes an act of generosity between strangers. Even time changes: appointments feel less urgent, kitchens warmer, books more inviting.

Perhaps that is why storms can be comforting. They briefly shrink the world to whatever is near—a roof, a room, a cup held between two hands. Beyond the glass, everything blurs. Inside, small things recover their importance.

And when the rain finally stops, the silence it leaves behind is not the same silence as before. It is cleaner somehow, full of dripping branches and reflected sky. The world has not been remade, exactly.

But it looks willing to begin again.
